name: Value Addition, Packaging and Agri-Marketing

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Making a product that pays

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing a value-added product
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare two value-added products for your farm and choose one with a real buyer.
This lesson builds toward: Given your farm's main crops or milk and what buyers near you ask for, you will choose one value-added product to make and the buyer to sell it to, after comparing at least two options on demand, raw material, equipment and rules.
Value addition means doing something to your produce that makes a buyer pay more: drying, milling, roasting, grinding, fermenting, cleaning, sorting into packs or simply packing it well. Fresh mangoes that rot in a week can become dried mango that keeps for months. Cassava can become flour or gari, groundnuts can become paste, and milk can become yoghurt.
Start with the buyer, not the machine. Ask shops, school cooks, hotels and market traders near you what they buy, how much, how often, in what pack size and at what price. A product nobody nearby is asking for is a risk.
Then check four things: demand (who will buy it and how much), raw material (do you or your neighbours have enough, all year or only in season), equipment and skill (can you start small, for example with a solar dryer or a hired mill), and rules (milk and meat products are higher risk and usually need more approvals than dry flour). Compare at least two options before you choose.
Step by step:
- List two or three products you could make from your own crops or milk.
- Ask at least three buyers what they buy, how much and at what price.
- Score each product on demand, raw material, equipment and skill, and rules.
- Choose the one with the best score and a named buyer.
Words to know:
- Value addition: changing or packing your produce so a buyer pays more for it.
- Shelf life: how long a product stays safe and good to eat.
- Perishable: a product that spoils fast, like milk, yoghurt or fresh tomatoes.
Try it now: Pick two products you could make. Ask three buyers near you about each one, then score both on demand, raw material, equipment and rules. Write down the product you choose and the buyer you will target.
You can now compare value-added products on demand, raw material, equipment and rules, and choose one with a real buyer.

check.q: You want to add value to your mangoes. What should you do first?
options: Buy a large dryer on credit
Ask buyers near you what they buy and at what price
Make as much as possible and look for buyers later
check.why: Starting with real buyers shows whether there is demand before you spend money.

check.q: Which product usually needs MORE approvals and care to make safely?
check.why: Milk products spoil fast and can carry germs, so they are higher risk and usually more tightly regulated.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Costing and pricing your product
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate the cost of one pack and set a price that covers every cost plus a margin.
This lesson builds toward: Given the costs of one batch, you will calculate the cost of one pack and set a selling price, counting raw material, packaging, energy, labour, transport and losses, with a price that covers every cost plus a margin.
Many small processors lose money without knowing it, because they only count the raw material. Count every cost of one batch: raw material, packaging and labels, energy (fuel, charcoal, electricity, milling fees), water, labour (including your own time), transport, and fees such as registration or market charges spread over the year.
Then count the losses: some product is spoiled, spilled or given as samples. Divide the total batch cost by the number of packs you can actually sell. Example (figures are examples only): a Ghana group makes groundnut paste. Groundnuts GHS 400, jars and labels GHS 150, milling and fuel GHS 50, labour GHS 100, transport GHS 50: total GHS 750. They fill 50 jars but expect to sell 48, so each jar costs about GHS 15.60.
Your price must cover the cost per pack plus a margin for profit, savings and repairs. Then check the price against similar products in shops. If your price is far above them, find a cheaper way to make it, a smaller pack, or a buyer who pays for quality. The same method works for dried mango in KES, gari in NGN or yoghurt in XOF.
Step by step:
- List every cost of one batch, including your own labour.
- Count how many packs you can really sell after losses.
- Divide the total cost by the packs you can sell: that is the cost per pack.
- Add a margin to get your price.
- Compare it with similar products in shops and adjust your plan if needed.
Words to know:
- Cost per unit: what it costs you to make one pack.
- Margin: the money left from each sale after costs are paid.
- Batch: one round of making the product, for example 50 jars made on one day.
Try it now: Make a cost sheet for one batch of your chosen product. List every cost, the packs you expect to sell, the cost per pack and the price you would charge. Compare it with one similar product in a shop.
You can now build a cost sheet, work out the cost of one pack and set a price that covers it with a margin.

check.q: Which cost do small processors MOST often forget?
check.why: Your own time and spoiled or sample packs are real costs, and leaving them out hides losses.

check.q: A batch costs KES 6,000 and you can sell 40 packs. What is the cost per pack?
check.why: Cost per pack is the total batch cost divided by packs sold: 6,000 / 40 = KES 150.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Hygiene and food safety when you process
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a hygiene checklist that keeps your product safe while you make it.
This lesson builds toward: For your chosen product, from processing to the buyer, you will write a hygiene and cold-chain checklist, covering hands, water, surfaces, raw material, packing and keeping the product safe in storage and transport.
A buyer will not come back, and an authority can stop your sales, if a product makes someone sick. The international Codex Alimentarius General Principles of Food Hygiene cover the whole chain, from the farm to the person who eats the food. Your national food body uses ideas like these when it inspects you.
The basics: clean, safe water; hands washed with soap before work and after the toilet; no work when you are sick; hair covered and cuts covered; clean surfaces, tools and containers; raw material kept apart from finished product; animals, insects and rats kept out; and a clean, dry place to store the packs.
Start with clean raw material. Never process mouldy groundnuts or grain, which can carry aflatoxin (see Post-Harvest Handling and Storage). Milk for yoghurt must be heated and handled using a tested method from your dairy extension officer or standards body, and kept cold. Write your steps down so every batch is made the same way, and give each batch a number and a date.
Step by step:
- Write the steps to make your product from raw material to sealed pack.
- For each step, write what could make it unsafe (dirt, germs, mould, insects).
- Write the hygiene rule that stops it.
- Give each batch a number and date, and record who made it.
Words to know:
- Food safety: keeping food free of germs, poisons and dirt that can make people sick.
- Contamination: when dirt, germs or chemicals get into food.
- Batch number: a code on each pack that tells you when and how it was made, so you can trace a problem.
Official sources:
- Codex Alimentarius (FAO/WHO): Committee on Food Hygiene and the General Principles of Food Hygiene (CXC 1-1969)
Try it now: Write the steps for making your product. Next to each step, write one thing that could make it unsafe and the rule that prevents it. This is your hygiene checklist.
You can now write a hygiene checklist for your product and give every batch a number and date.

check.q: A worker has diarrhoea on processing day. What should happen?
options: They stay away from processing until well
They work but wash hands once
check.why: Sick workers can pass germs into food, so they should not handle it until they are well.

check.q: Some groundnuts in a sack look mouldy. What do you do?
options: Roast them longer to kill the mould
Remove and do not use them for paste
Sell them at a lower price
check.why: Mould can carry aflatoxin, which cooking does not remove, so mouldy nuts must not be used.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Packing, labelling and selling direct

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Packaging, labels, branding and registration
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Draft a label for your product and find the national body that must approve it.
This lesson builds toward: Given your product and your country, you will draft a label and name the national body that must approve the product, with the product name, ingredients, net weight, producer and contact, batch number and dates, and a note to check the body's current rules.
Good packaging keeps the product safe and makes buyers trust it. Choose food-grade packs that keep out air, water and insects: sealed bags for dried mango and flour, clean jars with tight lids for groundnut paste, and clean, sealed cups for yoghurt. Your brand is your name, logo and promise, for example 'clean, local, no added sugar'. Keep it simple and the same on every pack.
A label usually shows: the product name, the ingredients, the net weight or volume, the producer's name and contact, the batch number, the date it was made and a use-by or best-before date, how to store it, and any registration number or mark. Your country may require more, so check before you print many labels.
Most packaged foods need approval before they are sold in shops. In Kenya, KEBS issues the Standardization Mark for products that meet a Kenya Standard. In Nigeria, NAFDAC registers locally made foods through its Made in Nigeria Food Division, with routes for small as well as medium and large producers. In Ghana, the Food and Drugs Authority registers products, and its Progressive Licensing Scheme lets very small producers (one to five people) meet the rules in stages. In Côte d'Ivoire, check with the national standards body CODINORM; other countries have their own. Rules, forms and fees change, so contact the body before you start.
Step by step:
- Choose a food-grade pack that keeps out air, water and insects.
- Write your brand name and one-line promise.
- Draft the label: name, ingredients, net weight, producer and contact, batch number, dates, storage.
- Find your national body (KEBS, NAFDAC, Ghana FDA, CODINORM or another) and ask what your product needs.
- Print labels only after you know the rules.
Words to know:
- Brand: the name, logo and promise that make buyers recognise and trust your product.
- Net weight: the weight of the food inside the pack, not counting the pack.
- Registration: official approval from a national body that a food may be sold.
- Best-before date: the date until which the product keeps its best quality if stored as the label says.
Official sources:
- Kenya Bureau of Standards (KEBS): Standardization Mark (product certification) and marks of quality
- NAFDAC (Nigeria): Food registration, Made in Nigeria Food Division (small and medium/large scale)
- Ghana Food and Drugs Authority: Product registration
- Ghana Food and Drugs Authority: Progressive Licensing Scheme for small producers (Pink, Yellow, Green)
Try it now: Draft the label for your product on paper or with a free tool like Canva. Then find the website or office of your national food body and write down the questions you will ask it about registration and labelling.
You can now draft a product label and name the national body to check with before you sell in shops.

check.q: Which item does a food label usually need?
options: The batch number and best-before date
check.why: Batch number and dates let buyers and inspectors know when it was made and how long it keeps.

check.q: A small Ghana processor with three workers wants FDA approval. Which programme can help them meet the rules in stages?
options: The Made in Nigeria Food Division
check.why: The Ghana FDA's Progressive Licensing Scheme is for small producers of one to five people.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Keeping the product safe on the way: cold chain and transport
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan how your product stays safe and undamaged from your store to the buyer.
This lesson builds toward: For your chosen product, from processing to the buyer, you will write a hygiene and cold-chain checklist, covering hands, water, surfaces, raw material, packing and keeping the product safe in storage and transport.
A product can be made perfectly and still spoil on the road. Perishable products such as yoghurt and fresh juice need a cold chain: they must stay cold at every step, from making to the buyer's fridge. If they warm up on the way, germs grow and the product can make people sick, even if it looks fine.
For short trips, use a clean cool box with ice packs and deliver early in the day. Agree with the buyer that they put it in a fridge at once. Never refreeze or re-sell yoghurt that has been warm. Dry products such as cassava flour, dried mango and groundnut paste do not need cold, but they must stay dry, sealed, shaded and away from fuel, chemicals and pests.
Plan the trip: who carries it, by what (motorbike, matatu, okada, bus or truck), how long it takes, and how packs are protected from crushing, sun and rain. Low-cost cooling such as FAO's zero energy cooling chamber can hold produce cooler before you process it. Write your cold-chain and transport steps onto your hygiene checklist.
Step by step:
- Decide if your product is perishable (needs cold) or dry (needs dry and sealed).
- For cold products: cool box, ice packs, early delivery, buyer's fridge at once.
- For dry products: sealed, shaded, away from chemicals and pests.
- Plan who carries it, how, how long, and how packs are protected.
- Add these steps to your hygiene checklist.
Words to know:
- Cold chain: keeping a product cold at every step from making it to selling it.
- Cool box: an insulated box that keeps things cold with ice or ice packs.
Official sources:
- FAO TECA/STI portal: Zero Energy Cooling Chamber for vegetables
Try it now: Write the journey of your product from your store to your buyer: who carries it, how, how long, and what keeps it cold or dry and undamaged. Add it to your hygiene checklist.
You can now plan a cold chain or dry transport route that keeps your product safe until the buyer has it.

check.q: Your yoghurt sat in the sun for three hours on a delayed bus. What do you do?
options: Sell it quickly at a discount
Put it back in the fridge and sell tomorrow
Do not sell it; it is no longer safe
Taste it and sell it if it seems fine
check.why: Warm yoghurt can grow germs that you cannot see or taste, so it should not be sold.

check.q: What does dried mango need most on the way to a buyer?
options: Kept next to the fuel can
check.why: Dry products spoil when they get damp, hot or near chemicals, not because they are warm.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Selling direct: shops, schools, hotels and online
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Prepare a pitch and written terms to sell your product direct to one buyer.
This lesson builds toward: Given one shop, school, hotel or online buyer, you will prepare a direct-selling pitch with written terms, stating the product, price, quantity, delivery, payment date and how complaints are handled.
Not every middleman is bad: some traders pay fairly and carry produce you cannot. But watch for warning signs of exploitation: rigged scales, prices changed after delivery, payment that comes months late or never, and 'buy now, pay later' from strangers who then disappear. Selling direct can give you a better price and a steady customer.
Each buyer wants different things. Local shops and supermarkets want a label, a steady supply and sometimes sell on consignment (they pay only after the product sells), which is a risk. Schools and hospitals buy in bulk on a schedule and often need a quote, an invoice and sometimes a registration. Hotels and restaurants want the same quality every time. Online buyers on WhatsApp, Facebook or a marketplace want clear photos, prices and quick delivery.
A good pitch is short: what the product is, why it is good (clean, local, fresh), the price, the pack size, how much you can supply and how often, and delivery. Then agree terms in writing, even in a simple message: quantity, price, delivery day, payment date and method (for example mobile money), and what happens if a pack is damaged. Keep a copy. Never share PINs or passwords with any buyer. For a big or long contract, ask a trusted adviser to read it first.
Step by step:
- Choose one buyer: a shop, school, hotel or online customers.
- Write a short pitch: product, why it is good, price, pack size, supply, delivery.
- Bring a sample and your label.
- Agree terms in writing: quantity, price, delivery, payment date and method, damaged packs.
- Keep a copy and record every delivery and payment.
Words to know:
- Middleman: a trader who buys from farmers and sells on to others.
- Consignment: the shop takes your goods and pays you only after they sell.
- Pitch: a short, clear offer to a buyer.
- Invoice: a written bill asking a buyer to pay for goods delivered.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page product plan. Include the product and buyer, your cost sheet and price, your hygiene and cold-chain checklist, your draft label and national body, and a short pitch with the terms you will ask the buyer to agree in writing.
You can now pitch your product to a direct buyer and agree clear written terms for price, delivery and payment.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Product and buyer A product is named with no buyer, or the choice was not compared with another option. One product and one named buyer, chosen after comparing two options on demand, raw material, equipment and rules. Also shows how raw material will be found all year, for example from neighbours or a group. Cost sheet and price Only raw material is counted, or there is no cost per pack. Every cost of a batch, including labour and losses, gives a cost per pack and a price with a margin. Price is checked against shop prices and the plan shows what to change if it is too high. Hygiene and cold chain No written steps, or key risks such as handwashing, mould or keeping it cold are missing. A checklist covers water, hands, surfaces, raw material, packing, batch numbers and safe transport. Each step names the risk and the rule, and someone else could follow it without help. Label and registration The label is missing ingredients, net weight, contact or dates, or no national body is named. The label shows name, ingredients, net weight, producer and contact, batch number, dates and storage, and names the body to check with. The learner has contacted the body and written down what it requires and what it costs. Pitch and terms No pitch, or no written terms for price, delivery and payment. A short pitch plus written terms: quantity, price, delivery day, payment date and method, damaged packs. The pitch was given to a real buyer, and the learner recorded the answer. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of the product plan and try again.

check.q: A shop offers to take your groundnut paste on consignment. What is the risk?
options: You must pay the shop first
You are paid only after it sells, and unsold packs may come back
The shop will change your label
There is no risk at all
check.why: On consignment you carry the risk until the product sells, so agree how long and what happens to unsold packs.

check.q: A hotel agrees to buy yoghurt weekly. What should you agree in writing?
options: Quantity, price, delivery day, payment date and what happens to damaged packs
check.why: Written terms on quantity, price, delivery and payment prevent disputes later.
